articles.text: General Grant is suffering with rheumatism in addition to his throat difficulty.
articles.summary: Brief note that General Grant is suffering from rheumatism as well as his throat ailment.

articles.text: Middleton is still in persuit of Big Bear and appears to be afraid that he will overtake him.
articles.summary: Sarcastic note that General Middleton is still pursuing Big Bear in the Northwest Rebellion.

articles.text: It is the opinion of Governor Pierce that the census which is being taken, will give Dakota a population of about 500,000.
articles.summary: Governor Pierce expects the census to show a Dakota population of about 500,000.

articles.text: The June Number of The Northwest is bright and newsy and has some very fine illustrations. Look in the next number for some descriptions of Medora.
articles.summary: The June number of The Northwest is praised; the next number will describe Medora.

articles.text: The annual letter of Lake Erie Seminary at Painsville, O., has just been received and shows a very prosperous condition of the seminary. The story of its twenty-fifth anniversary will soon be issued and will be very interesting.
articles.summary: Notice of the annual letter of Lake Erie Seminary, Painesville, Ohio.

articles.text: The Montana Stock Gazette is a new stock paper being published at Billings Mont., by the Gazette Publishing Co. It is a bright, wide-awake, newsy eight page paper. F. W. Brandt is the duly authorized collecting agent of the company.
articles.summary: Notice of the new Montana Stock Gazette at Billings; F. W. Brandt is its collecting agent.

articles.text: The promised prosperity does not seem to have come with the new administration at Washington. Times were never more stringent in the east than they are today. There is plenty of money but it is all locked up in the vaults of the New York banks.
articles.summary: Editorial remark that the new administration has not brought prosperity and money is locked up in New York banks.

articles.text: The quarantine craze is nearly as violent as the roller skating mania. Poor, dear, old Michigan has finally concluded that the veterinary surgeons (?) of that state need a "lift" and is coming into line with a quarantine law a yard long. Rhode Island and D. C. are yet to be heard from.
articles.summary: Editorial jab at the cattle quarantine craze, citing Michigan's new quarantine law.

articles.text: In the June Century appears an article by Hon. Theo. Roosevelt describing his hunting expedition to the Big Horn mountains last fall. It is a very interesting account and has received favorable comment from many leading Journals. Three very fine engravings accompany the article.
articles.summary: Notes Theodore Roosevelt's article in the June Century on his Big Horn mountains hunting trip of the previous fall.

articles.text: The first 500 cattle from the H S outfit have been slaughtered and are on their way to market. The next bunch will be delivered Sunday or Monday, and from that time on, the house will be run to its fullest capacity. The first consignment although not all that could be desired, were good beef and will doubtless find a ready market.
articles.summary: The first 500 H S cattle have been slaughtered at the Medora abattoir and shipped; the house will soon run at full capacity.

articles.text: Col. J. N. Simpson received a telegram from one of his foremen last week saying that their first drive of 6,500 head of Texas cattle passed Dodge City on the old trail all right. There were 30 or 40 other herds waiting to see which way the H S cattle went, and are now following. This looks as if the quarantine business was something of a failure.
articles.summary: Col. J. N. Simpson's first drive of 6,500 Texas cattle passed Dodge City, with 30 or 40 herds following.

articles.text: The special car of the Northwest magazine, laid at Medora from Friday evening till Saturday night. There were on board Messrs. E. V. Smalley, editor of the Northwest, T. F. Kane and H. H. Lemont. A number of views of the town and abbatoirs were taken and will appear with full descriptions in subsequent numbers of the magazine. This paper has no rival in its descriptions of the Northwest and its industries.
articles.summary: The Northwest magazine's special car stopped at Medora with E. V. Smalley, T. F. Kane and H. H. Lemont, who took views of the town and abattoirs.

articles.text: Some tenderfoot Sunday School Superintendent signing himself "Pony Bill," writes to the Stock Grower in a lackadaisical sort of way (two long columns) about "Round-up No. One," giving the Cowboys a lot of taffy about their good looks, store clothes, and "sich" and winds up with the following moral. "To the credit of cowboys be it printed that none of the cowboys of round-up number one were seen drunk in Glendive yesterday or today. Continue on that line boys and Pony has hopes and friendship for you all." Come Marney, this is very fatiguing, while it is still fresh in our memory how you insisted on retiring to your room in our sanctum, by the way of the fire escape and the skylight, the last time you were in Medora.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy ribs 'Pony Bill' for his Stock Grower letter praising the sober cowboys of Round-up No. One at Glendive.

articles.text: "There is nothing in our stock Journals now days," is a remark made in our hearing a few days since by one of the most prominent stock-growers of the northwest. The worst feature about this remark is, that there is too much truth in it. Whose fault is it? Why yours Mr. Editor of course. You fill up your paper with clippings which if not always stale are often of more interest to yourself than your readers. You are not careful enough to find out what your reader wants to know. You also write articles from half a column to two columns long, when you ought to know, if you do not, that the average stockman will not read an article that is over a quarter of a column in length. Give us short articles and to the point. Why cannot stock papers have an associated press report of their own, and get stock news from one section of the country to another before it gets stale by being copied from one paper to another? Many of your readers have interests in Texas, Colorado, Dakota and Montana. We don't know much your about your way of getting up a newspaper, but we do know when we get news and when we don't.—[Stockgrower.
articles.summary: Reprint from the Stockgrower complaining that stock journals print stale clippings and overlong articles.

articles.headline: STOCK NOTES. Annoncement.
articles.text:
Cattle-men of the Little Missouri river are advised that the Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car Company, will give them during June for the beef and dry cows that they wish to sell, Chicago prices less seventy cents per hundred to cover freight and shrinkage. The cattle to be delivered in the evening at the Sully Creek corrals and weighed in the morning.

articles.text: Nelson Storey of Bozeman Mont., has one of the finest herds of Polled-Angus cattle in the northwest and they came through the winter in as fine shape as any of the native range cattle.
articles.summary: Nelson Story's Polled-Angus herd at Bozeman wintered well.

articles.text: Our Mingusville correspondent says the round-up reached there the 30th, and started towards Glendive Sunday morning. Wm. Fly whose cattle were held at Sentinel Butte on account of quarantine, shipped his stock Sunday evening, consisting of twenty-four car loads. There has been plenty of rain around Mingusville this spring and cattle are reported in very good condition. The prospects are that shipments of cattle will begin at Mingusville about the middle of July.—[Stockgrowers' Journal.
articles.summary: Round-up reached Mingusville on the 30th; Wm. Fly shipped 24 carloads from Sentinel Butte after quarantine.

articles.text: Brill & Osgood are to start a new industry in Miles City by way of experiment. That is canning beef. The firm have fifty or sixty barrels of beef ready for cooking and canning as soon as the cans arrive. There will be about 3,000 cans of the beef put up for the home market, and sold to the merchants at the same price they can purchase from any of the canned beef establishments. By way of experiments, Messrs. Brill & Osgood put up a small quantity of beef in home made cans, and it has turned out bright, sweet, and very palatable, and was preferred to that sold by the old-established houses. We hope that Messrs. Brill & Osgood will succeed in their endeavors and add another important industry to those already established here.—[Stockgrowers' Journal.
articles.summary: Brill & Osgood plan an experimental beef-canning industry at Miles City.

articles.text: There has probably never been a time in the history of thorough-bred cattle in the United States, when they could be purchased at such low figures as at the present time. There is no reason now why range cattle should not be bred to a higher standard. The objection may be advanced, that the higher bred stock will not stand privation because it is not invested with as much vitality as natives. This objection is undoubtedly to some extent well founded, as that is an end that has not been sought by breeders to any great extent up to the present time. The man who produces an animal especially adapted to the range, and popular in the eastern markets will have a fortune at his command. An animal possessing the instincts of the Texas cow, and the body of nearly any of the high bred cattle barring the Jersey, would very nearly meet the demand.
articles.summary: Comment that thoroughbred cattle are cheap and range cattle should be bred up.

articles.headline: HITTING THE INSPECTORS.
articles.text:
Scene at Trinidad: Ranchman arrives from the land of blue grass with 115 head of Shorthorns, which he presents for inspection.

Inspector—"Whar you from?"
Ranchman—"Kentucky."
Inspector—"What you got?"
Ranchman—"Shorthorn cattle."
Inspector—"Got any Texas fever?"
Ranchman—"No."
Inspector—"How many you got?"
Ranchman—"115 head."
Inspector—"All right, dollar a head."
Money paid, and then:
Ranchman—"I suppose you will give me a clean bill of health?"
Inspector—"Oh, them cattle is all right stranger, jist trot 'em through."—[Ex.
articles.summary: Humorous exchange piece about a Trinidad cattle inspector passing Kentucky shorthorns for a dollar a head.

articles.headline: SMILES.
articles.text:
"JOSIAR."

I never kin forget the day
That we went out a-walkin',
And sot down on the river bank,
And kept on hours a-talkin';
He twisted up my apron strings
An' folded it together,
An' said he thought for harvest time
'Twas cur'us kind o' weather.

The sun went down as we sot there;
Josiah seemed uneasy,
And mother she began to call:
"Loweezy! O Loweezy!"
An' then Josiah spoke right up
As I was just a startin',
An' said, "Loweezy, what's the use
Of us two ever partin'?"

It kind o' took me by surprise,
An' yet I knew 'twas coming;
I'd heard it all the summer long
In every wild bee's hummin';
I'd studied out the way I'd act;
But law! I couldn't do it;
I meant to hide my love from him,
But seems as if he knew it;
In looking down into my eyes
He must a seen the fire;
An' ever since that hour I've loved
An' worshiped my Josiar.
—Exchange.

THE COWS ARE ALL RIGHT.

Grocer—I wish you wouldn't frighten your cows, my lad; it makes the butter pale.

Farmers Boy—Yes; but it wasn't the cows that was skeered.

Grocer—Your mother told me that you frightened the cows, and that was the cause of the butter being so white. Come now; confess, didn't you scare the cows?

Boy—Skeer nothin'! Mam was givin' you taffy. The cat jumped into the churn and skeered the butter, but the cows is all right.—[Newsman Independent.

MARRIAGE IN ARIZONA.

"Do you take this woman whose hand you are a-squeezin' to be your lawful wife, in flush times an' skimp?"

"I reckon that's about the size of it, squire."

"Do you take this man you've j'ined fists with to be your pard through thick an' thin?"

"Well, you're about right for once, old man."

"All right, then. Kiss in court, an' I reckon you're married about as tight as the law j'ine you. I guess four bit 'll do, Bill, if I don't have to kiss the bride. If I do, it's six bits extra."—[Chicago Ledger.
articles.summary: 'Smiles' humor column: the dialect poem 'Josiar,' 'The Cows Are All Right' and 'Marriage in Arizona,' all credited to exchanges.

articles.headline: THE LOST CABIN GOLD MINES. By J. S. WARN.
articles.text:
During the day they sent a man to explore the valley for signs of Indians. Finding the coast clear they struck camp and started for the head of the stream up in the mountains, prospecting as they went, wherever there was any signs of colors. When they arrived near the mountains they made a permanent camp, in order to give the numerous gulches a thorough prospecting, and if possible find the source of the colors which they had panned out on the sand bars along the river. They constructed breast works and dug trenches in order to protect themselves against attacks from the Indians. Every thing being in readiness they began digging and struck bed rock in about seven feet. They found gold from the grass roots down, from five cents to one dollar to the pan. The men were nearly fantic over their success, after so many long years of fruitless toils. Having fully satisfied themselves that they had at last realized their long cherished hopes, they at once began preparations for mining in good earnest. They whip-sawed lumber for sluice boxes and run a dam across the creek which was near at hand, dug a ditch and set their boxes, and then worked all the dirt from the top down, finding it very rich, realizing from fifty to one hundred dollars per day to the man. This was in the month of September. They worked for a month and took out large quantities of dust. Mr. Hulburt could not tell exactly how much but thought it would measure a good "half bushel."

As it was now getting rather late in the season, they set about preparing for winter quarters for themselves and their animals. They cut hay and built a stockade with their cabin in one corner and had everything in first class shape for cold weather. All kinds of game were plenty and the brooks were filled with speckled trout, and they looked forward to a comfortable winter. All went well for several months.

In the spring of '64 as the snow was melting off the ground and the hill-sides were getting bare, the water was running in the creeks, and every one was in good spirits and full of activity, setting sluice boxes and getting ready for the summers work. After they had been at work about a week, just before night Hulburt went to the cabin to get supper, and as he was busily engaged he heard the report of several rifles in the direction of the mine. Running to the door he saw his comrades weltering in their blood and the red-skins scalping them and stripping them of their buckskin clothing. The Indians then started for the cabin but the bold miner kept them at bay until dark, and thinking that they had him safely corralled, did not renew the attack until the next morning.

(Continued.)
articles.summary: Serial installment by J. S. Warn of the Lost Cabin gold mines story: Hulburt's party strikes rich gold, winters over, and is attacked by Indians in spring 1864.

articles.summary: J. M. Hannigan and wife went east Wednesday morning for a month's visit.

articles.summary: Patrick O'Hara of the Medora coal Co. bought Mrs. Julia Lason's house in Little Missouri and will move it to Medora.

articles.text: One of our young lady friends made a flying trip to Glendive last week, returning Monday morning. It is rumored—but we wont give it away.
articles.summary: Teasing note on a young lady's flying trip to Glendive.

articles.text: Messrs. Miller, Rose and Rouse of Clevland, O., are visiting the Bad Lands with a view of locating a cattle ranch. Mr. Miller will for the present stop with Col. Moore at his ranch.
articles.summary: Messrs. Miller, Rose and Rouse of Cleveland are looking to locate a cattle ranch; Miller is staying with Col. Moore.

articles.text: The N. P. Ref. Co. have shipped two cars dressed beef daily since last Friday. They will get cattle from the round-up sufficient to supply the demand until the fifteenth, when the next bunch will be delivered by the H S outfit.
articles.summary: The N. P. Refrigerator Co. has shipped two cars of dressed beef daily since Friday; the H S outfit will deliver the next bunch on the 15th.

articles.text: A severe frost Sunday night killed nearly all the peaches. Some fears are entertained that other fruits have also suffered, although it is hoped that gooseberries and bananas are still safe. Cowslips and horse chestnuts are out of danger.
articles.summary: Joking report of a hard frost Sunday night that killed the peaches.

articles.text: East bound trains on the Northern Pacific railroad for the past week have been occasioned by a bad wash-out on the west fork of the Gallatin about 400 yards long, necessitating transfer of passengers and baggage by wagon seven miles.
articles.summary: A 400-yard wash-out on the west fork of the Gallatin has disrupted eastbound Northern Pacific trains.

articles.text: Jos. U. Rose treasurer of the LeMoyne Cattle Co., who has been with the round-up a few days, returning to Pittsburgh Pa. Tuesday. This company will receive a consignment of cattle in a few days. Next year their herd will be largely increased.
articles.summary: Jos. U. Rose, treasurer of the LeMoyne Cattle Co., returned to Pittsburgh after time with the round-up; the company expects more cattle.

articles.text: It was decreed that the celestials must go and they went. Yak Wah, finding that naturalized citizens were more popular than heathen in Medora, concluded to pack up his "laumly" and emigrate to some place where the climate was more serene.
articles.summary: Yak Wah, the Chinese laundryman, has left Medora.

articles.text: Al. Canter says he don't mind so much the going up, but it is the coming down that hurts. We did n't suppose there was anything with hair on that could lay Al. in the sand, but he says himself that it was a straight, square bounce and he don't care who knows it.
articles.summary: Al. Canter was thrown from a horse.

articles.text: Hon. Fredrick Billings passed through here today in his special car en route for Portland. The boys over on the west side say that some of the ladies on the car gave them tracts. It is to be hoped they will read them as we do not know of a more promising (?) field than Little Missouri for missionary work.
articles.summary: Frederick Billings passed through Medora in his special car bound for Portland; ladies aboard handed out tracts.

articles.text: "Thou art so near and yet so far," is the title of a new poem by Seth Weyland, dedicated to the prize rifle. There is not room for the whole poem this week as it has 99 verses, but the nub of the story is, that "one is afraid and the other daresn't." Come boys, if you are afraid to shoot against Seth's score, just say so and quit.
articles.summary: Joke about Seth Weyland's poem on the prize rifle and a shooting challenge.

articles.text: The Medora bucket brigade fire company behaved very handsomely at the fire last evening. Probably several million dollars of property would have been destroyed if it had not been for the assistance of this valuable organization. They have a very fine assortment of fire appliances and are a fine looking body of men—probably.
articles.summary: Mock-praise of the Medora bucket brigade at a fire last evening.

articles.text: Marquis de Mores had a very narrow escape from drowning last Tuesday afternoon. As he was fording the river just above the bridge on horse-back, his horse got mired in the quick-sand. The Marquis dismounted to help the horse and in the struggle got under his feet. The horse finally got loose and made for the shore, leaving the Marquis standing on a sand bar in the middle of the river, and obliging him wade out.
articles.summary: The Marquis de Mores nearly drowned Tuesday afternoon when his horse mired in quicksand while fording the river above the bridge.

articles.summary: Notice to freighters to take watches to the King jeweler at Spearfish or Deadwood.

articles.headline: LOST.
articles.text: Al. Canter foreman of the Bad Lands Cattle Co., lost a rawhide lariat near mouth of Box Elder, it was on a VI horse, he will pay $10 on its return to this office by the finder.
articles.summary: Al. Canter of the Bad Lands Cattle Co. lost a rawhide lariat near the mouth of Box Elder; $10 reward.

articles.summary: Drug Store notice for glassware.

articles.summary: Messrs. Ingram and Wilson of Mandan were in town this week.

articles.text: A fine lot of Silver plated-ware will soon be opened at the Drug Store.
articles.summary: Drug Store notice for silver plated-ware.

articles.text: The well by the company's office has been supplied with a force pump 40 man power. Bro, Cole will now have something with which to occupy his many leisure moments, squirting water on trees and grass that have lately been planted in "the Park."
articles.summary: A force pump was put on the well by the company's office; Cole will water the trees in 'the Park.'

articles.text: Charlie Ellison has at last seen "the cow that jumped over the moon," or thinks he has, which is all the same, only in this case it was a Texas steer instead of a cow. They say Charlie's face was a study for an artist about the time the steer's fore legs cleared the cantle of the saddle.
articles.summary: Charlie Ellison was thrown by a Texas steer.

articles.text: Round-up No. 6 arrived at Medora Sunday evening on the west side of the river. The high water prevented working the last eight miles on the east side of the river. They returned Wednesday and worked the unfinished country and then proceeded down the river. The percentage of calves branded thus far is not very satisfactory.
articles.summary: Round-up No. 6 reached Medora Sunday evening, worked unfinished country after high water, and moved down river; calf branding is unsatisfactory.

articles.text: Our school is progressing finely, and the teacher is all that could be expected. the new board of directors is composed of men who are bound to have a good school or none. They are a "heap better rustlers" than the former directors and are determined that the children shall not grow up in superstition and ignorance. Gentleman accept our congratulations.
articles.summary: The Medora school is progressing under a new board of directors.

articles.text: Fred. Banan went to Fort Keogh last Sunday night where he will remain for two months to complete his term of enlistment, and then return to his shop at Medora. Mr. Butler will preside at the chair until Fred. sends a man to relieve him. We might here make some remarks, but will defer them until Jim's. relief comes as the fighting editor is not at home.
articles.summary: Barber Fred. Banan went to Fort Keogh to finish his enlistment; Mr. Butler takes his chair.

articles.text:
A visitor to our sanctum this morning, laboring under the exhilarating influence of a slight attack of tangle-foot, expressed himself as follows, in regard to the abbatoirs of Medora. "Zhe odors 'rising from zhe decayed carcasses of defunct animals az zhe slaughter-house int'posing 'tween zhe pure a'm'sph'r 'n my olfact'ry nerves, izh very det'men'al to my plezzure. S'long zhen'lm'n." The devil did not recover in time to get in the "dull sickening thud" racket.

Scene in the Park.

Doctor Timlin, step this way a few moments and examine the gentleman's wounds.

Patient. Izh it very bad doc'r?

Doctor. Them's my elucidations. Can't live over fifteen minutes at the outside. Very bad scalp-wound, three sixteenths of an inch long. Take 93 stitches to fix it. 'Taint worth while to monkey with it. Better make your will.
articles.summary: Comic sketch of a tipsy visitor complaining of the abattoir smells, followed by 'Scene in the Park' with Doctor Timlin.
